problem: “a few roods of land” rendered “a few acres”: a rood is a quarter acre, so the figure is inflated and the smallness of the aim is lost.
replacement: The taste for physical gratifications leads a democratic people into no such excesses. There the love of well-being appears as a tenacious, exclusive and universal passion, but its range is narrow. No one thinks of building enormous palaces, of conquering or imitating nature, or of ransacking the world to satisfy one man’s passions. The aim is rather to add a few roods of land to your field, to plant an orchard, to enlarge a house, to keep making life more comfortable and convenient, to avoid trouble, and to meet the smallest needs without effort and almost without cost. These are small objects, but the soul clings to them. It dwells on them closely, day after day, until at last they shut out the rest of the world and sometimes come between the soul and heaven.

problem: “momentary outbreaks” became “sudden outbreaks”; the idea of brevity is lost.
replacement: Although the desire to acquire the good things of this world is the dominant passion of the American people, there are certain brief outbreaks when their souls seem to burst the bonds of matter that hold them and soar impetuously toward heaven. In all the States of the Union, but especially in the half-settled country of the Far West, you meet wandering preachers who peddle the word of God from place to place. Whole families, old men, women and children alike, cross rough passes and untrodden wilds, coming from a great distance to join a camp meeting. There, for several days and nights, they forget entirely the cares of business and even the most pressing needs of the body as they listen to these sermons. Here and there in American society you meet men full of a fanatical and almost wild enthusiasm that hardly exists in Europe. From time to time strange sects arise that try to cut out extraordinary paths to eternal happiness. Religious insanity is very common in the United States.

problem: Last sentence is left as a fragment after “but” (“but before he has tired of…”); awkward English.
replacement: In the United States a man builds a house to spend his later years in, and sells it before the roof is on. He plants a garden and rents it out just as the trees are beginning to bear fruit. He brings a field into cultivation and leaves others to gather the crops. He takes up a profession and gives it up. He settles in a place and soon leaves it, to carry his changeable longings elsewhere. If his private affairs leave him any free time, he plunges at once into the whirlpool of politics. And if, at the end of a year of unceasing labor, he finds he has a few days’ vacation, his eager curiosity sweeps him across the vast expanse of the United States, and he will travel fifteen hundred miles in a few days to shake off his happiness. Death finally overtakes him, but it comes before he has tired of his fruitless chase after that complete happiness which is forever on the wing.

problem: Term drift: “make no condition permanent” rendered “make no position permanent” (conditions must not become position/status).
replacement: At first sight there is something surprising in the strange unrest of so many happy men, restless in the midst of abundance. Yet the sight itself is as old as the world. What is new is to see a whole people provide an example of it. Their taste for physical gratifications must be regarded as the original source of the secret uneasiness that the actions of the Americans betray, and of the inconstancy of which they give fresh examples every day. A man who has set his heart exclusively on the pursuit of worldly welfare is always in a hurry, for he has only a limited time to reach it, to grasp it and to enjoy it. The memory of how short life is spurs him on constantly. Besides the good things he has, he imagines at every moment a thousand others that death will prevent him from trying if he does not try them soon. This thought fills him with anxiety, fear and regret, and keeps his mind in ceaseless agitation, which leads him to change his plans and his home again and again. Suppose that, in addition to the taste for physical well-being, there is a social condition in which laws and customs make no condition permanent. That is a powerful further stimulus to this restless temper. Men will then be seen constantly changing their course, for fear of missing the shortest way to happiness. It is easy to see that men passionately bent on physical gratifications desire eagerly, but are also easily discouraged. Their final aim is to enjoy, so the means of reaching it must be quick and easy, or the trouble of getting the gratification would be greater than the gratification itself. Their usual frame of mind is therefore both ardent and slack, violent and enervated. Death is often less dreaded than persevering in continuous effort toward a single end.

problem: “the number of those who partake in them is larger” sharpened to “many more people share in them”.
replacement: Among democratic nations men easily attain a certain equality of conditions, but they can never attain the equality they desire. It is always drawing back from them, yet without hiding from their sight, and as it draws back it draws them on. At every moment they think they are about to seize it, and at every moment it slips from their hold. They are near enough to see its charms but too far away to enjoy them, and they die before they have fully tasted its delights. To these causes we must attribute the strange melancholy that often haunts the inhabitants of democratic countries in the midst of their abundance, and the disgust with life that sometimes seizes them in calm and easy circumstances. In France people complain that the number of suicides is rising. In America suicide is rare, but insanity is said to be more common than anywhere else. These are all different symptoms of the same disease. The Americans, however uneasy they may be, do not end their lives, because their religion forbids it. Among them materialism may be said hardly to exist, despite the general passion for physical gratification. The will resists, but reason often gives way. In democratic ages pleasures are more intense than in aristocratic ages, and above all the number of those who share in them is larger. But on the other hand, it must be admitted that man’s hopes and desires are more often crushed, the soul is more stricken and disturbed, and care itself is sharper.

problem: “the amount of productive industry is checked” sharpened to “the volume of productive industry falls off” (checked is not necessarily a fall).
replacement: When a democratic state turns into an absolute monarchy, the activity that used to be directed at both public and private affairs is suddenly concentrated on private affairs alone. The immediate result, for a time, is great physical prosperity. But this impulse soon slackens, and the amount of productive industry is held back. I do not know whether a single trading or manufacturing people can be named, from the Tyrians down to the Florentines and the English, that was not also a free people. There is therefore a close bond and a necessary relation between these two elements, freedom and productive industry. This proposition is generally true of all nations, but especially of democratic nations. I have already shown that men who live in ages of equality constantly need to form associations in order to obtain the things they want. I have also shown how greatly political freedom improves and spreads the art of association. In these ages, then, freedom is especially favorable to the production of wealth. It is not hard to see that despotism is especially hostile to the same result. The nature of despotic power in democratic ages is not to be fierce or cruel, but petty and meddling. Despotism of this kind, though it does not trample on humanity, is directly opposed to the spirit of commerce and the pursuits of industry.

problem: Hedge sharpened: “it may be supposed that these passions are united” became “must be supposed”.
replacement: Up to now the Americans have fortunately escaped all the dangers I have just pointed out, and in this respect they truly deserve admiration. Perhaps there is no country in the world where fewer idle men are to be found than in America, or where all who work are more eager to promote their own welfare. But if the Americans’ passion for physical gratifications is violent, at least it is not indiscriminate. Reason, though unable to restrain it, still directs its course. An American attends to his private concerns as if he were alone in the world, and the next minute he gives himself up to the common good as if he had forgotten them. At one moment he seems driven by the most selfish greed, at another by the most lively patriotism. The human heart cannot be divided in this way. The inhabitants of the United States show, by turns, so strong and so similar a passion for their own welfare and for their freedom that it may be supposed these passions are united and mingled somewhere in their character. And indeed the Americans believe their freedom to be the best instrument and surest safeguard of their welfare. They are attached to the one because of the other. They by no means think that they are not called on to take part in the public good. On the contrary, they believe that their chief business is to secure for themselves a government that will allow them to acquire the things they want, and will not bar them from the peaceful enjoyment of the possessions they have acquired.
